strengths: The paper proposes a clear and interesting post-hoc approach for VLM uncertainty: estimating density of normalized embeddings on the hypersphere using conditional Riemannian flow matching, then using negative log-density as an uncertainty score.
The method is well motivated geometrically: VLM embeddings are typically l2-normalized, and the comparison to Euclidean flow variants supports the value of respecting the spherical manifold.

The empirical selective-classification results are broad across six datasets, three proxy datasets, and an additional SigLIP backbone, with consistent gains in Acc@90% rejection over ProbVLM and MC dropout in many settings.

The paper includes useful ablations on geometry, proxy dataset size, and ODE integration steps, as well as reasonable implementation details for the vector-field architecture and training hyperparameters.

The limitations section acknowledges an important fairness risk: density-based uncertainty may flag underrepresented populations or rare domains as high uncertainty due to data sparsity rather than actual model error.
weaknesses: The central claim that embedding negative log-density is a principled epistemic uncertainty measure is not adequately supported. The theoretical chain relies on strong and mostly unverified assumptions: local linearity in parameters, the claim that training suppresses parameter-Jacobian norm specifically in high-density regions, and an implausible near-isometry/change-of-variables argument from high-dimensional inputs to lower-dimensional embeddings. These steps are heuristic rather than a rigorous foundation.

The evaluation does not convincingly establish epistemic uncertainty rather than density, typicality, or semantic frequency. Low-density embeddings can correspond to rare but correctly handled concepts, minority subpopulations, or domain shift; the paper does not disentangle these from true model ignorance or validate against Bayesian/ensemble epistemic uncertainty beyond limited baselines.

The main selective-classification metric is weakly chosen and overclaimed. Spearman correlation between rejection fraction and retained-set accuracy can easily be near 1 whenever accuracy monotonically rises with rejection, and it is not the same as correlation between uncertainty and individual prediction error. More standard risk-coverage metrics such as AURC/E-AURC, AUROC for error detection, calibration curves, and coverage at fixed risk are missing.

The OOD and data-curation applications are under-evaluated. The OOD section shows distributions and curves but reports no AUROC/AUPR/FPR@95 numbers, and the data-curation claim is based only on qualitative examples without showing that filtering improves downstream training, retrieval, or classification.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives hyperparameters and architecture sketches, but does not specify code availability, exact sampling procedures, seeds, hardware cost/training time, prompt templates for zero-shot classification, MC dropout implementation details, or enough baseline-training details to ensure fair replication. There is also a confusing inconsistency between saying 1M pairs are sampled/trained and later saying Table 2/Figure 2 use 500K pairs.

The computational comparison is not fully convincing. REPVLM requires training an additional flow model for 400k steps on up to hundreds of thousands or millions of proxy pairs, but the cost table focuses only on inference GFLOPs and largely omits training/storage cost and the cost of constructing proxy embeddings.

The presentation sometimes overstates the evidence, using phrases such as “near-perfect correlation with model error” and “rigorous link” despite the above methodological caveats. There are also minor clarity and polish issues, including typos, table/section inconsistencies, and missing quantitative values in figures.

strengths: The core idea of modeling normalized VLM embeddings on the hypersphere with Riemannian flow matching is plausible and relevant, and the paper connects an active density-estimation technique to an important practical problem: uncertainty scoring for frozen VLMs.

The method is described at a reasonable algorithmic level, with appendix derivations, architecture details, hyperparameters, proxy datasets, and some ablations over geometry, proxy data size, and ODE steps.

The empirical tables show consistent improvements in Acc@90% rejection over MC dropout and ProbVLM on several selective classification benchmarks, and the method appears computationally cheaper than repeated full-backbone dropout passes.
weaknesses: The central claim that negative embedding log-density is a principled measure of epistemic uncertainty is not convincingly supported. The theoretical argument relies on unjustified steps: the optimality condition does not imply small parameter-Jacobian norm in high-density regions, the encoder is not an invertible change-of-variables map from inputs to embeddings, and the local/dynamical isometry assumption for pretrained VLMs is asserted rather than tested.

The evaluation metric called Spearman's S is not a direct correlation between sample uncertainty and prediction error, despite the paper repeatedly claiming near-perfect correlation with errors. It is described as correlation between rejection fraction and retained accuracy, which can be nearly monotonic for many scores and is much weaker evidence than AUROC/AUPRC for error detection, risk-coverage AURC, ECE, or calibration curves.

The experiments do not isolate epistemic uncertainty from data rarity, domain mismatch, image quality, or proxy-dataset density. A low-density embedding under CC/DataComp/LAION may simply indicate underrepresentation in the proxy data, not model ignorance; this is acknowledged only briefly as a limitation but undermines the interpretation of the method.

The OOD and data-curation applications are under-evaluated. Figure 4 shows curves but no quantitative AUROC/AUPRC/FPR95 values, and the data-curation claim is supported only by qualitative examples rather than demonstrating improved downstream training or cleaning performance.

The baseline comparison is narrow and potentially unfair. Important confidence and selective-classification baselines for CLIP-style zero-shot models, such as maximum softmax/similarity margin, energy scores, kNN or kernel density in embedding space, Mahalanobis distance, nearest-neighbor distance to proxy embeddings, and OOD scoring methods, are absent. Without these, it is unclear whether a costly flow model is needed.

Several technical statements are questionable. The paper repeatedly calls the likelihood exact, but inference uses learned vector fields, Hutchinson trace estimation, and coarse Euler integration. The Riemannian divergence simplification from manifold divergence to ambient trace is also not sufficiently justified for an extrinsically parameterized projected vector field.

The proxy-data setup raises possible leakage and interpretability concerns. OpenCLIP ViT-B/32 is trained on LAION-scale data, while LAION-derived proxy data is also used for the density model; evaluation datasets may overlap or be represented in these corpora, and the paper does not analyze contamination or how proxy choice affects conclusions.

Presentation has notable gaps and overclaims. The paper says results use 1M proxy pairs but also states Table 2/Figure 2 use 500K pairs; the SigLIP appendix reference is written as Appendix 10; some figures lack precise numeric reporting; and claims such as 'reliable tool for high-stakes selective classification' are too strong for the evidence.

Reproducibility is incomplete: there is no code release mentioned, dataset sampling details and zero-shot prompt templates are missing, runtime/wall-clock costs are absent, and the exact statistical protocol for the five seeds is unclear. The limitations and ethics discussion notes a fairness risk but does not evaluate or mitigate it.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: scalable epistemic uncertainty estimation for frozen VLMs, where common Bayesian or ensemble methods are expensive and probabilistic embedding methods mostly address aleatoric uncertainty.

The core idea of estimating density on the hyperspherical embedding manifold is natural, and the use of conditional Riemannian flow matching is technically well matched to normalized CLIP/SigLIP embeddings.

The empirical results are broad for selective classification: multiple downstream datasets, three proxy datasets, two VLM backbones, and comparisons against MC dropout and ProbVLM. REPVLM usually improves Acc@90% rejection substantially, especially under distribution shift such as ObjectNet and ImageNet-R/Sketch.

The paper includes useful ablations on Riemannian versus Euclidean flow matching, proxy dataset size, and ODE integration steps, plus a computational cost comparison showing that the method is much cheaper than MC dropout.
The limitations section honestly notes dependence on representative proxy data and the fairness risk that sparse demographic regions may be assigned high uncertainty.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification is suggestive rather than rigorous. The chain from parameter-Jacobian norm to input density to embedding density relies on strong assumptions, including local linearity, optimization suppressing Jacobians in high-density regions, and approximate local isometry of contrastive encoders. These assumptions are not empirically validated and do not fully establish that negative log embedding density is epistemic uncertainty rather than novelty or typicality.

The main metric, Spearman correlation between rejection fraction and accuracy, is weak evidence for the claim of near-perfect correlation with prediction error. It appears to correlate aggregate accuracy with rejection level rather than directly correlating per-sample uncertainty with correctness, and many monotone rejection curves can yield near-perfect values. More standard selective prediction metrics such as AURC, risk-coverage curves, AUROC/AUPR for error detection, calibration/error detection statistics, and confidence intervals over examples would make the claim more convincing.

The baseline set is incomplete. For a density/embedding-space method, comparisons to simpler post-hoc alternatives such as kNN distance/density in embedding space, Mahalanobis or Gaussian mixture density, CLIP softmax confidence/energy, maximum similarity margin, and conformal/selective baselines are important. Without these, it is unclear how much benefit comes from Riemannian flow matching specifically versus generic embedding typicality.

The OOD and data curation applications are under-evaluated. OOD detection is shown mostly with plots and qualitative claims but no clear AUROC/AUPR/FPR95 table; data curation is only qualitative and does not show that filtering improves downstream training or dataset quality.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper gives datasets, hyperparameters, architecture sketches, and compute, but there are inconsistencies such as 1M proxy samples versus main results reportedly based on 500K, and residual block depth described as both 8 and 6. Code availability, exact prompts/templates for zero-shot classification, preprocessing details, random sampling protocol, and baseline implementation details are not sufficiently specified.

There may be dataset overlap or dependence concerns: using LAION/DataComp/Conceptual Captions as proxy density data with OpenCLIP trained on LAION-like corpora could make the uncertainty score partly reflect pretraining-data coverage in uncontrolled ways. This is relevant to the epistemic interpretation but not deeply analyzed.

The method may misclassify rare but valid samples as high uncertainty because it is density-based. The paper acknowledges this fairness issue, but the empirical evaluation does not measure subgroup behavior or harms on underrepresented concepts/domains.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: post-hoc epistemic uncertainty for frozen vision-language models, where ensemble or dropout-style approaches are expensive and probabilistic embedding methods mostly target aleatoric uncertainty.

The core idea of estimating density directly on the hypersphere of normalized VLM embeddings using conditional Riemannian flow matching is technically interesting and more geometry-aware than Euclidean Gaussian or GMM density baselines.

The empirical section is fairly broad for selective classification: multiple proxy datasets, several downstream benchmarks, comparisons to MC dropout, ProbVLM, embedding norm, W-CLIP, GMM, and conformity scores, plus ablations on geometry, proxy data size, and ODE steps.

The paper is unusually candid in its limitations: it acknowledges that the density-to-epistemic-uncertainty link is a proxy argument, that proxy dataset choice matters, that the method assumes normalized cosine-style embedding geometry, and that density-based curation can create fairness risks.
Presentation is generally clear, with a coherent method description, useful diagrams/tables, and appendices giving algorithmic and architectural details.
weaknesses: The central claim that the method provides epistemic uncertainty is not fully supported. The theoretical chain relies on strong assumptions, especially the pointwise Jacobian-density link and the empirical assumption that embedding density preserves input/data support. These are explicitly not proven, so the paper should frame the method more cautiously as an embedding-density confidence score rather than a principled epistemic uncertainty estimator.

The main evaluation metric is problematic. Spearman correlation is computed between rejection fraction and retained-set accuracy, not directly between per-sample uncertainty and prediction error. Because accuracy often increases monotonically as samples are rejected, many methods obtain S near 1.0, so the reported 'near-perfect correlation' overstates the evidence. More standard selective prediction metrics such as AURC, E-AURC, risk-coverage curves, calibration/error-detection AUROC, and sample-level uncertainty-error correlations are needed.

The empirical advantage is less decisive than claimed. Simple baselines such as embedding norm and conformity match or outperform REPVLM in several cells, especially on Food101, ObjectNet/LAION, ImageNet-Sketch, and the SigLIP results. The SigLIP appendix shows substantial degradation on in-distribution benchmarks, which weakens the claimed generality across VLMs.

The OOD detection and data curation sections are under-evidenced. The OOD section shows distributions and curves but does not report quantitative AUROC/AUPR/FPR95 values or compare to strong OOD baselines. The curation result is qualitative only and does not demonstrate that filtering improves downstream training, stability, or data quality at scale.

There are reproducibility concerns. The manuscript says code is available but leaves the location blank, and there is an inconsistency between the main text saying REPVLM is trained on 1M pairs from each proxy dataset and Appendix B.1 saying Table 2/Figure 2 use 500K pairs. Important implementation details for likelihood estimation, random seeds, exact baseline configurations, and compute/training time are not sufficient for reliable reproduction.

The likelihood computation needs more mathematical care. The paper claims exact log-density from the learned Riemannian flow while using Euler integration, Hutchinson estimates, tangent projection, and renormalization. The stated simplification of Riemannian divergence to Euclidean divergence for tangent fields is not sufficiently justified and may depend on the chosen extension of the vector field off the manifold. This matters because the uncertainty score is the estimated log-density.

The comparison to epistemic uncertainty baselines is limited. MC dropout and ProbVLM are included, but no deep ensemble, Laplace/linearized approximation, test-time augmentation, conformal/selective prediction baselines, or CLIP-specific confidence baselines based on softmax margins/energy are reported. This makes it hard to isolate whether density estimation is the decisive factor.

The method inherits known failures of density models for OOD and rarity detection. The paper acknowledges rarity/fairness risks, but the evaluation does not include subgroup analysis or tests where rare valid examples should not be rejected, despite recommending data curation as an application.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: scalable epistemic uncertainty estimation for frozen vision-language models, where ensembles or repeated stochastic inference can be expensive.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is not soundly established. The proposed chain from Bayesian epistemic uncertainty to parameter-Jacobian norm to data density to embedding density relies on strong assumptions, and the manuscript itself concedes that the key density-preservation step for non-invertible contrastive encoders is only an empirical assumption. This makes the claim that negative log embedding density is a principled epistemic uncertainty measure substantially overstated.

The main evaluation metric is problematic. The paper describes Spearman's S as the correlation between rejection fraction and accuracy, not between per-example uncertainty and prediction error. This can become nearly 1.0 whenever an accuracy-rejection curve is monotone, and many simple baselines also obtain S=1.000. Thus the reported near-perfect correlations do not convincingly demonstrate calibrated epistemic uncertainty or error prediction.

Empirical evidence is weaker than the claims. REPVLM is not consistently best: simple baselines such as Embedding Norm or Conformity outperform or match it in several Acc@90 cells, especially Food101 and some shift settings. The SigLIP appendix shows substantial degradation and even negative correlations on in-distribution benchmarks, which undercuts the generality of the method.

The OOD and data-curation applications are under-evaluated. OOD detection is mostly shown through plots without clear AUROC/AUPR/FPR95 numbers or baseline comparisons, and data curation is qualitative only. Claims that filtering high-uncertainty samples improves future training are speculative and not experimentally validated.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Although the appendix gives some training details, important items remain underspecified, including exact proxy-data sampling/filtering, implementation details for baselines, seeds/splits, prompt/template variants, ODE solver settings beyond step count, and the manuscript contains an unfinished 'code available at' statement with no repository link.

The method's originality is moderate. Riemannian flow matching and density estimation on hyperspherical embeddings are known ingredients; the paper's contribution is mainly their application to VLM uncertainty. The manuscript does not clearly show that the more complex flow model is necessary compared with simpler density/geometric scores, given the mixed baseline results.

The presentation overclaims. Phrases such as 'exact log-density,' 'near-perfect correlation with model error,' and 'rigorous link' are not justified by the approximations, Hutchinson estimates, Euler integration, and weak theoretical assumptions. The limitations section is helpful, but it does not sufficiently temper the conclusions throughout the paper.

Ethical limitations are acknowledged, especially the risk that density-based curation conflates rarity with ignorance, but the paper does not provide subgroup analyses or safeguards. This is material because the proposed data-curation use case could remove rare but valid samples.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: scalable epistemic uncertainty quantification for frozen vision-language models, where ensembles or parameter-space Bayesian methods are often impractical.

The core idea of estimating embedding density directly on the hypersphere with conditional Riemannian flow matching is well motivated and technically coherent. Respecting the normalized embedding geometry is a natural design choice, and the ablations show consistent gains over Euclidean variants.

The empirical evaluation is broad for selective classification: multiple proxy datasets, several downstream benchmarks, CLIP and SigLIP-style backbones, repeated runs, and comparisons to MC dropout, ProbVLM, embedding norm, W-CLIP, GMM, and conformity-style baselines.
The method appears computationally practical at inference time. The reported overhead of roughly 0.55 GFLOPs beyond the frozen backbone is a useful advantage over MC dropout-style approaches.

The paper is unusually careful in its limitations discussion. It explicitly acknowledges that the density-uncertainty link is a proxy argument rather than a formal identity, that proxy data matters, that assumptions are tied to normalized contrastive encoders, and that density-based curation can create fairness risks for rare but valid samples.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim remains substantially assumption-driven. The chain from Bayesian epistemic uncertainty to parameter-Jacobian norm to input density to embedding density contains weak links, especially the pointwise Jacobian-density relation and the empirical assumption that contrastive embedding density preserves input/data coverage. The paper is honest about this, but the theory should be viewed as motivation rather than support for a strong epistemic-uncertainty claim.

The main metric labeled as Spearman correlation is problematic. The paper defines Spearman's S as correlation between rejection fraction and retained-set accuracy, yet table captions describe it as correlation between uncertainty and prediction error. This is not the same as a per-example uncertainty-error correlation and may explain the many saturated 1.000 values, including for simple baselines. This weakens the claim of near-perfect correlation between uncertainty and model error.

Some headline empirical claims are stronger than the evidence supports. REPVLM is often best or near-best, but simple baselines such as embedding norm and conformity are highly competitive and sometimes better in Acc@90, especially on Food101, ObjectNet/LAION, and ImageNet-Sketch. The gains are useful but not uniformly dominant.

The OOD and data curation sections are under-quantified. The OOD experiment shows score distributions and mean ROC/PR curves but does not report AUROC/AUPR/FPR95 values or compare against baselines. The curation result is qualitative only, with no downstream training or cleaning experiment demonstrating actual benefit.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript. Hyperparameters, datasets, backbone identifiers, and architecture sketches are provided, but the text leaves the code URL blank, does not fully specify implementation details for baselines, and relies on large proxy datasets and A100-scale training, which may make independent reproduction nontrivial.

The applicability boundary is material: results on SigLIP are mixed, with degraded in-distribution performance and even negative reported Spearman values in some cells. This suggests the method is most convincing for CLIP-like contrastive normalized embeddings rather than VLMs broadly.

There are some technical presentation issues in the likelihood derivation. The manifold divergence simplification and Hutchinson estimator treatment are terse, and the inference algorithm uses renormalized Euler steps rather than a more principled exponential-map integrator, so the claim of exact log-density is somewhat overstated in practice.
